Johannes Kessler
yō-han'nes kes'ler
n. (Johannes Kessler, 1502–1574, saddler, reader and preacher at St Gallen, chronicler of the Reformation)
Latin Johannes, from Hebrew Yochanan, the LORD is gracious; Kessler, a coppersmith, a maker of kettles.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Johannes Kessler was a St Gallen boy sent to study at Wittenberg, and on the road in March 1522 he and a companion fell in at the Black Bear inn at Jena with a knight in a red cap reading a Hebrew psalter, who paid for their supper and questioned them about Wittenberg; it was Luther coming down from the Wartburg, and Kessler's account of the evening is the best-known eyewitness page in Reformation literature. He came home to a city that could not pay him as a preacher, so he learned the saddler's trade and worked at it for twenty years while teaching the Scriptures in the artisans' reading-schools of St Gallen, where craftsmen met to have the Bible read and expounded. He wrote the Sabbata, a chronicle of the Swiss Reformation as he saw it. Only in 1542 was he given a regular charge, and in 1571 he became the city's chief pastor. A tradesman who taught the Bible at a workbench for two decades. “And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought” (Act 18:3).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a saddler as one whose occupation is to make saddles, and a chronicle as a historical account of facts in order of time.

expand to see more

SAD'DLER, n. One whose occupation is to make saddles.

CHRON'ICLE, n. A historical account of facts or events disposed in the order of time.

AR'TISAN, n. One trained to manual dexterity in some mechanic art or trade; a handicraftsman.

EXPOUND', v. To explain; to lay open the meaning; to interpret.

Key Scripture

Act 18:3 — "And because he was of the same craft, he abode with them, and wrought: for by their occupation they were tentmakers."

Act 20:34 — "Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities, and to them that were with me."

1Th 2:9 — "For ye remember, brethren, our labour and travail: for labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God."

Act 18:26 — "And he began to speak boldly in the synagogue: whom when Aquila and Priscilla had heard, they took him unto them, and expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly."

Modern Corruption

The saddler who taught Scripture at a workbench and met Luther at an inn.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The live misuse is the modern use made of the St Gallen reading-schools by those who argue from them that the church needs no ordained ministry, since artisans read and expounded the Bible among themselves. Kessler himself sought and eventually accepted a regular call, and the reading-schools operated under the city's ministers, not instead of them.

The principle to recover is that a man who must earn his bread with his hands is not thereby disqualified from teaching, and that the apostles set the precedent on purpose: “Yea, ye yourselves know, that these hands have ministered unto my necessities” (Act 20:34). Paul tells the Thessalonians why he did it: “labouring night and day, because we would not be chargeable unto any of you, we preached unto you the gospel of God” (1Th 2:9).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek homotechnos (G3673), of the same trade; skenopoios (G4635), a tentmaker.

Usage

"“he abode with them, and wrought” (Act 18:3) — twenty years at the saddler's bench."

"“these hands have ministered unto my necessities” (Act 20:34) — a preacher the city could not pay."

"“expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly” (Act 18:26) — the reading-schools of St Gallen."
